name: Accounting policy — what it is and how one is selected
definition: An accounting policy is the specific accounting principle, and the method of applying that principle, adopted by an enterprise in preparing and presenting financial statements. No single list applies to all circumstances; the choice calls for judgement by management, and is governed by Prudence, Substance over Form and Materiality, with a true and fair view as the primary consideration.
why_it_exists: Two enterprises can record the same transaction differently and both be correct, because more than one principle is acceptable. That is only tolerable if the choice is disciplined and disclosed. This concept fixes what the choosable thing is, so that a later change to it can be identified as a change in policy rather than something else.
inputs: the class of transaction or event to be accounted for
the acceptable alternative principles and methods of applying them
the circumstances of the specific enterprise
outputs: a selected accounting principle and the method of applying it, for that class
preconditions: financial statements are being prepared and presented by an enterprise
more than one acceptable principle or method exists for the class of transaction
exceptions: UNKNOWN — AS 1 does not state when a selection is foreclosed by another standard; not extracted from this source
common_mistakes: treating a chosen method as universal when AS 1 states there is no single list applicable to all circumstances
selecting a treatment on its legal form when substance and form differ
anticipating a profit before it is realised, which Prudence forbids, while omitting provision for a known liability whose amount is only estimable
legal_references: UNKNOWN — statutory backing not extracted; only ICAI AS-1 and AS-5 were read for this claim, so no statute is cited
gst_references: NOT APPLICABLE — AS-1 and AS-5 govern financial-statement policy and period attribution; GST is a separate determination and must not be conflated with it
evidence_required: the principle and the method of applying it, stated for the class of transaction
the facts of the transaction as distinct from its legal form, where the two differ
confidence_factors: weak when the document shows the legal form only and nothing about the substance of the arrangement
AS 1 gives no numeric threshold for 'material' — it is defined by influence on a user's decision, which is not measurable from a document alone
the standard assigns the choice to management judgement, so a selection cannot be derived from the transaction alone
validation_checks: the treatment applied is the enterprise's stated policy for that class, not an ad hoc choice
no profit is recognised that has not been realised
a known liability or loss carries a provision even where the amount is only a best estimate
examples: depreciation, inventory valuation and treatment of goodwill are areas AS 1 names as ones where different enterprises adopt different policies

evidence.quote: The accounting policies refer to the specific accounting principles and the methods of applying those principles adopted by the enterprise in the preparation and presentation of financial statements.
There is no single list of accounting policies which are applicable to all circumstances.

The choice of the appropriate accounting principles and the methods of applying those principles in the specific circumstances of each enterprise calls for considerable judgement by the management of the enterprise.
The following are examples of the areas in which different accounting policies may be adopted by different enterprises.
Methods of depreciation, depletion and amortisation
The above list of examples is not intended to be exhaustive.

The primary consideration in the selection of accounting policies by an enterprise is that the financial statements prepared and presented on the basis of such accounting policies should represent a true and fair view of the state of affairs of the enterprise as at the balance sheet date and of the profit or loss for the period ended on that date.
For this purpose, the major considerations governing the selection and application of accounting policies are

In view of the uncertainty attached to future events, profits are not anticipated but recognised only when realised though not necessarily in cash. Provision is made for all known liabilities and losses even though the amount cannot be determined with certainty and represents only a best estimate in the light of available information.
The accounting treatment and presentation in financial statements of transactions and events should be governed by their substance and not merely by the legal form.
items the knowledge of which might influence the decisions of the user of the financial statements.
